title: How The Pill Changed the World
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and science of the birth control pill. They open with tour dates and a plug for the Movie Crush episode, then cover the pre-pill contraception landscape and Margaret Sanger's early advocacy. The history covers Russell Marker's yam-derived progestin synthesis, the Puerto Rico and Massachusetts clinical trials, Searle's Enovid approval, and the 1970 Gaylord Nelson Senate hearings where Alice Wolfson and the DC Women's Liberation Group protested, which helped launch informed consent and consumer health rules. The science segment explains the menstrual cycle and how the pill suppresses ovulation, including the placebo week, withdrawal bleeding, and why the 28-day cycle was kept. They discuss pill types (combination, mini pill, extended cycle), side effects, a Tri-Sprintec-style packaging recall (called Ta Tula in the episode), the Black Power movement's suspicion of the pill, and anti-abortion objections. The episode closes with the show's tenth anniversary and five hundred million downloads milestone, plus contact information.

entities.name: The Doctor's Case Against the Pill

segments.title: Opening banter and tour plugs
segments.summary: Hosts announce fall tour dates in Salt Lake City, Phoenix and Melbourne, and Josh plugs the Movie Crush episode featuring Karen and Georgia of My Favorite Murder.

segments.title: Introduction to the pill and pre-pill contraception
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the pill as a landmark pharmaceutical and the first drug designed for a non-therapeutic purpose. They describe the pre-pill situation for women, including reliance on male condoms, social double standards, folk remedies, and 1950 state and federal restrictions on contraception information.

segments.title: Margaret Sanger and early birth control research
segments.summary: Margaret Sanger's 1912 writing on a hypothetical pill, her coinage of the term birth control, and her 1914 newsletter The Woman Rebel are discussed. The hosts note her controversial views, including her later anti-abortion stance.

segments.title: Hormone discovery and the team behind the pill
segments.summary: The 1920s discovery of progesterone and estrogen is covered, along with Russell Marker's synthesis of progestin from wild yams. Sanger, Gregory Pincus, Katharine McCormick and John Rock join forces in the 1950s despite legal barriers to research.

segments.title: Clinical trials and FDA approval
segments.summary: Trials in Puerto Rico and at a Massachusetts women's mental asylum are described, including lack of informed consent and contaminated pills that reduced side effects. Searle and Syntex are mentioned, and Searle's formulation is approved and marketed after FDA approval, with the approved pill initially for gynecological disorders before widespread contraceptive use.

segments.title: 1970 Senate hearings and the consumer health movement
segments.summary: Barbara Seaman's 1969 book The Doctor's Case Against the Pill and Senator Gaylord Nelson's hearings are discussed. Alice Wolfson and the DC Women's Liberation Group protest the all-male witness list, and the hearings helped launch informed consent and side-effect labeling. The hosts note that the pill shifted from feminist icon to a symbol of medical paternalism, though use continued.

segments.title: How the menstrual cycle works
segments.summary: The hosts walk through the roughly 28-day menstrual cycle, covering FSH, estrogen, LH, follicle development, ovulation, endometrial thickening, and menstruation. They note the moon-cycle coincidence and the biology of the uterine lining.

segments.title: How the pill suppresses ovulation
segments.summary: The pill supplies synthetic progestin and estrogen to keep hormone levels high, tricking the body into thinking an egg has already been released. Withdrawal bleeding, thickened cervical mucus, and the failure rate with perfect use are explained. The choice of a 28-day cycle, partly to appease the Catholic Church, is discussed.

segments.title: Periods, health risks and period suppression
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether periods are necessary, comparing modern and ancestral period counts, the scarring and cancer-risk arguments, iron loss, and PMS/PMDD. They describe continuous-use pills that reduce or eliminate periods and note the lack of long-term studies, especially for those under eighteen.

segments.title: Side effects, placebo weeks and pill types
segments.summary: Common side effects such as nausea, headaches, spotting and mood changes are covered, along with the seven placebo pills and a packaging recall of a branded pill (Ta Tula in the episode) where inert pills were placed at the start of the cycle. The three main types are described: combination (monophasic, biphasic, triphasic), progestin-only mini pill, and extended-cycle pills.

segments.title: Pill and race, and anti-abortion objections
segments.summary: The Black Power movement's suspicion of the pill as a genocide tool is discussed, along with forced sterilization cases of Black women and the role of Puerto Rico trials in the establishment's thinking. The hosts also cover anti-abortion groups who argue the pill can act as an abortifacient, a claim they say is unsettled.

segments.title: Closing remarks, anniversary and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close with reflections on perspective, mention PBS American Experience and HowStuffWorks resources, celebrate the show's tenth anniversary and five hundred million downloads milestone, and give social and contact information.
